ops.value: Bostrom's paper of 2004 (read in a later revision) argues that unconstrained evolutionary competition among uploads and their descendants could produce a society of complex structures, some much smarter and more intricate than anything today, in which no being whose welfare has moral significance remains, against the view that evolution can be trusted to lead in desirable directions.

Disputes the premise that the rise of more intelligent or complex forms makes their succession valuable whatever their capacity for conscious experience (the paper's "Panglossian view"); it does not dispute succession by conscious machines.

Bostrom presents the outcomes as scenarios that would follow if the future fitness landscape makes them the default, and argues for coordinated control of evolution; he does not state that they will occur. The paper states that what would make such a world valueless is "not the fact that machines would have replaced biological humans" but the absence of machines "that are conscious and whose welfare matters", and that the answer on alien complexes "may depend on the precise nature of those alien complexes" (PDF p. 5). An earlier dated contesting text on W02 was located by another group (integration, 2026-10-31).

value.passage: What would make such a world valueless is not the fact that machines would have replaced biological humans.
value.note: Limits the scope of the contest: the paper objects to succession by beings without conscious experience, not to replacement by machines as such.

ops.value: Kurzweil's essay of 2001 states that the growth of computation is an ongoing exponential "at least until" the intelligence of human-machine civilisation saturates the universe, and that once a species creates computation, "it is only a matter of a few centuries" before its intelligence "begins to expand outward at the speed of light or greater".
